name: Khamba
confidence_why: Nothing describes Khamba word stress: the only first-hand remark is a one-page 2016 CIIL-SPPEL project flyer whose preliminary analysis notes "tonal features" and states that no linguistic research on the language exists, while Badu 2002 (Memba of Mechuka, a sister variety) lists only consonants and vowels and Tournadre and Suzuki 2023 have no Khamba entry.

catalog_locator: single page, right column, section 'The Language'
catalog_quote: Preliminary analysis of Khamba data (phonology and clause), as expected, shows that Khamba is attributed with typological features of Tibeto-Burman language spoken in Northeast India, for example, the clausal structure of Khamba has a SVO pattern and tonal features are noticed. A Tibetan script is used for literary work. Kagiu Boom, Yokar and Tengur are some of the books written in Khamba using a Tibetan Script. No linguistic research or documentation has done yet on this language.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is stated anywhere. The only first-hand prosodic remark on Khamba proper is CIIL-SPPEL's preliminary field observation that the language shows tonal features; stress/accent placement is not mentioned in any accessible source (the one accessible phonology page, Badu 2002 on the closely related Memba of Mechuka, lists segments only).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is a preliminary project note, not a phonological analysis; no word/phrase domain given. Family-level context only (Tournadre & Suzuki 2023 sec. 7.3.3-7.3.4: in tonal Tibetic/Kham varieties pitch is primary and the first two syllables form a trochaic strong-weak unit) -- not specific to this language.
new_statements.identity_note: Target is Khamba [kbg] proper: c. 500-1,300 speakers in Nyering, Nyukong, Yortong, Mankota, Tasigong, Singha, Shimoling (Singa circle / Yang Sang Chu valley, Tuting subdivision, Upper Siang). The only accessible source with a 'Phonology' section, Badu 2002, describes MEMBA of Mechuka (West Siang/Shi-Yomi), a closely related Bodish variety with no ISO code of its own that Glottolog files under kham1283 ('Memba of the Mechuka valley =.. very similar to Khamba [kbg]'); Akanksha 2022 likewise describes Memba. Do not confuse with the Khamba of Manipuri literature (Khamba-Thoibi) or Khams Tibetan [khg] 'Khampa'.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the record held by the project (SPPEL 2016 Khamba flyer: 'tonal features are noticed', no word-stress statement; catalog classification undetermined): tone asserted, nothing on stress, so nothing changes and the kind stays undetermined. Identity caveat, material: the thesis describes Memba of the Mechuka (Menchukha) valley, Shi-Yomi district, self-name Nehnangi/Bazashiriba, and itself treats the 'Khambas of Upper Siang' as a different Buddhist group 'who speak their own distinct languages' (ch. 2) and the Tuting/Gelling 'Membas' as Tshangla speakers (ch. 1 p. 2); Glottolog files Mechuka Memba under kham1283 ('very similar to Khamba'), but the catalog's Khamba record (SPPEL, Yan…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The thesis gives a segmental phonology (29 consonants, 7 vowels, vowel length, syllable types, clusters) and only asserts in passing that Memba has tone as a suprasegmental (implicitly contrastive) feature, tagging three lexical items '(TONE)'; it offers no tonal analysis and says nothing at all about word stress or accent placement.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the only 'stress' in the thesis is a generic morphology-textbook remark (ch. 4 pp. 127-128, Hindi examples) that lexical morphemes can take stress and grammatical morphemes cannot, not a claim about Memba
new_statements.identity_note: Akanksha 2022 describes Memba of the Mechukha (Menchukha) valley, Shi-Yomi (formerly West Siang) district; Glottolog files Memba references under kham1283 ('very similar to Khamba') but the catalog's Khamba [kbg] is the language of the Yang Sang Chu valley near Tuting (Upper Siang). Any statement eventually taken from the thesis should be labelled Memba (Mechukha).
